abstract: Bacteria engage in many cooperative behaviours which provide benefits to other cells in the population. Lab experiments have suggested that these costly behaviours can be favoured by kin selection due to the benefits they provide to closely related cells. However, we know much less about the role of kin selection in natural populations. Here, we used two complementary methods to measure and compare kin selected signatures of cooperation in 19 species of bacteria found in the guts of honey bees. We used bioinformatic tools to count the number (and proportion) of genes for cooperative traits in a genome, and used molecular population genetics to measure how natural selection is acting on those genes. We found evidence for a consistent signature of kin selection for cooperation on genes controlling cooperative traits across species. Genes for cooperative traits had more non-synonymous relative to synonymous polymorphism than genes for private traits, had more protein-changing mutations and more codons under positive selection, and were lost more often. From this signature, we estimate an average relatedness of 0.73 between interacting cells. However, we found no evidence supporting the prediction that this signature varies with relatedness estimated from metagenomes. These patterns suggest that whilst genes for cooperative traits are undergoing kin selection in natural populations, there may be other factors influencing how the action of kin selection varies across species.
